The beeping was getting faster and louder in Captain Hudson’s ear. His eyelids snapped open and he ripped the oxygen mask off his face. Hudson twisted the latch, opening his pod, or coffin as the crew had come to call them. The door to his pod let out a pressurized hiss as the seal was broken for the first time in five years. He tried to climb out, but the needle in his arm administering the IV fluid forced him back. Wincing, he carefully pulled the needle out and plugged the puncture with his fingers. Hudson thrust his way to the cockpit as he floated past the flashing lights and beeping alarms. Reaching the cockpit, he twisted himself down in the pilot’s chair and clipped himself in.

The control panel in front of and above him was flashing like a Christmas tree, alternating red and white flashes. He tried to reach NASA on the communications system, but the only sound coming from his headset was the echoed feedback of the alarms on his ship. The digital diagram of the ship showed extensive damage to the port side wing and the nose cone had almost been completely sheared off. Hudson popped the button to the seatbelt with his fist and pushed himself to the port-aft window to observe the damage. The wing had deep, clean gashes through what he approximated to be 80% of the top and front face. It was an odd sight. If this were on earth, he thought, there’d be no way that wing would still be intact. The lack of atmosphere had mostly kept the shredded wing intact. For now.

Pushing himself through the passages of the ship, Hudson reached the crew quarters and pulled the emergency release latches on the pods of his remaining crew members one by one. Dr. Wu was the first to emerge. He could see the panicked look on Hudson’s face. Wu skipped the small talk and one-liner quips he was known for and cut right to the chase.

“How bad is it?” Wu said as he ran his finger along the library of binders filled with the most meticulous step-by-step instructions to fixing almost every possible problem they could encounter. He was looking for the Physical and Structural Damage Manuals. Thompson, the ship Engineer and by all measures the smartest person on board climbed out of her pod and immediately thrust herself toward the port window. As Hudson gave the impromptu situation report, Thompson let out an audible gasp as she realized just how bad the damage was.

“We’ll lose the port side wing. It’s still there for now, but when we hit atmosphere it’s gone. Nose cone is sheared off. We lost all comms with NASA, no radar, no telemetry. We’ll have to do this on our own,” Hudson said with a slight quiver in his voice as he forced the knot in his throat back down. He was scared and Wu and Thompson could tell. Hudson was selected as Commander of this mission mainly because of his previous two fly-by volleys around Phobos before it disintegrated and was swallowed by Mars’ atmosphere, but also because of his history as a POW of the Orbital War and his ability to deal with the stress and the pressures of the job.

Part 2 of 3

The three crew headed back up to the cockpit and fastened themselves in their respective seats. Hudson in the pilot’s chair, Thompson to his right sat in the co-pilot’s chair, and Wu was tethered in the sling behind the two pilots. He needed to move quickly from control panel to control panel and opted not to strap in to the chair, but tethered himself to the ceiling trackline.

“Thompson, figure out how far out we are. Wu, how are the thrusters?” Hudson ordered, trying to remain calm as he took manual control of the ship, disabling the autopilot. “Stern thrusters are go. Starboard thrusters go. Port thrusters no go. Bow thrusters go,” Wu replied as he bounced back and forth between panels.

“Sir, we’ll be entering Martian Atmosphere in approximately 30 minutes,” Thompson replied as she was still punching in computations on the terminal in front of her. The Advanced EmDrive Propulsion System NASA had been using for the past few years still took some getting used to for nearly all the astronauts. Time and distance no longer seemed to matter as much. Space flights now only took one sixth of the amount of time. A 30 year trip to Mars has now become a five years trip. This was the first manned trip to Mars using the EmDrive system and hyperbaric hibernation system.

The pock-marked, iron-oxide surface of Mars was becoming more and more clear as the ship got closer and closer. It was beautiful really and the three astronauts couldn’t help but quickly admire the view as they hoped they’d be the first humans to step on Martian soil.

Hudson pumped the bow thrusters gradually and manually disabled the EmDrive. The EmDrive had to be manually disabled as it was designed to run at full propulsion until the ship reaches atmosphere. At which point a series of high powered thrusters would burn off their fuel cells to bring the ship down to a safe landing. If the ship in its capacity were to enter atmosphere under full EmDrive throttle, Hudson believed the ship would be broken up piece by piece and mostly burnt up in the process. Besides, Hudson knew he needed those landing thrusters now more than ever, but he needed them to power on before they entered atmosphere, not after.

This posed an extreme risk as the fuel cells were only designed to last the exact amount of time necessary to fully enter Martian atmosphere and make a safe landing. Firing up the thrusters before entering the atmosphere would most certainly be the equivalent of killing the engines of a jet-liner 30,000 feet up and hoping for a soft landing.

“Hudson, are you sure that’s a good idea?” Thompson questioned his decision as she knew the risks and the possible outcome as well. She knew exactly what he was planning to do, but despite not agreeing with the plan, she could not come up with a better idea.

Wu was grabbing procedure manual after manual, rifling through the pages and then dropping it to grab another when he couldn’t find what he was looking for. Wu wasn’t quite sure what he was looking for, but he knew he had to find something. There had to be something there about attempting a hard manual landing.

Part 3 of 3

“You got a better idea? Let me hear it, Lieutenant.” Hudson said. Thompson didn’t reply.

“Five minutes to atmosphere,” Thompson reported. Hudson fired the landing thruster ignitors.

“Firing landing thrusters, hold on tight,” Hudson ordered. The ship seemed to float momentarily above the Martian atmosphere as the thrusters kicked on.

“Entering Martian atmosphere in 30 seconds. Wu, strap in now!” Thompson yelled. Wu hurriedly untethered himself from the ceiling trackline, and kicked off the wall toward his chair behind Thompson. As he grabbed the armrest, the craft suffered a jarring and violent pop. The sudden change in momentum was enough to send Wu flying head first into the control panel in front of Hudson and then into the back of the ship as the ship tried to recover. Wu bounced like a pinball against the walls of the ship finally colliding neck first into the corner of the crew passageway. The collision was enough to break his C3 vertebrae, killing him instantly. Once the ship had mostly recovered, Wu’s lifeless body came tumbling back toward the cockpit as the Martian gravitation pull reeled the ship in.

“Wu!” Thompson shouted and in an instant she had popped her seat belt and climbed back to his body.

“Thompson I need you up here with me!” Hudson ordered. The ship suffered another violent jolt as the port side wing slowly peeled back and released into the Martian sky like a metal banana peel. As the wing disintegrated, the ship began to spin violently out of control. Hudson struggled to straighten the craft, manipulating the direction and intensity of the thrusters. Finally righting the ship, he called back to Thompson.

“Thompson! Get up here!” The panic was setting in. Hudson quickly glanced behind him to see Thompson fastening Wu’s body into its seat.

“Thirty seconds of cell life on those thrusters Hudson, find some place to set us down easy!” Thompson gave the orders this time as she strapped herself back into her seat. Hudson struggled to keep the ship level and out of a violent spin. It took all his mental and physical strength to maintain the controls and timing of the thrusters.

“Ten seconds. I’ll see you when the dust settles.” Hudson said to Thompson. They both counted down in their heads silently. The ship was level and Hudson believed he had it set to coast into the Martian soil. However, without radar, it was impossible to predict exactly the type of terrain they would encounter. 5, 4, 3, 2, Thompson closed her eyes.

Impact. The ship landed hard but relatively flat on the rocky soil. The existing starboard wing clipped the ground as the ship bounced along causing the ship to flip end over end like a child’s toy airplane being thrown across the ground. The cabin windshield shattered as it toppled end over end. The ship was breaking up into pieces, scattering them across the desolate red dirt.

Thompson screamed inside her helmet as she opened her eyes just in time to see Hudson being ripped from the cockpit, his chair with him strapped in bouncing along. She could see the terrain ahead closing in quickly and she knew this was bad news. The ship continued to roll until it finally came to a stop, the open cockpit smashing head first into the side of a cliff.

Thompson was alive. She looked down to assess the damage. Her right foot had been completely turned the opposite direction from a compound fracture of the talus bone below her ankle. The adrenaline was flowing and the pain had yet to set in. She popped her seatbelt and moved to stand up only to find out she couldn’t. She toppled forward in pain landing head first on a softball sized rock. The faceplate to her helmet was cracked and as she looked down at her ankle the crack spider-webbed out from the pressure inside her suit. “No, no, no, no! Please God, no!” She cried as her suit began to beep indicating low oxygen. She tried to crawl back to the crew quarters but she did not have the strength.

“Ten percent oxygen remaining,” the voice inside her helmet reminded her. She continued to sob, pleading for her life.

“Five percent oxygen remaining,” the voice said calmly. Thompson sniffled and stopped her tears. She began thinking about her life and the people she’d leave behind. She remembered the good times, her husband, John, and their two children, Michael and Sarah. She tried to replay the memories in her head but all she could do was picture their faces, smiling at her.

“Oxygen depleted,” the voice replied one final time. This isn’t how it was supposed to happen, thought Thompson. I’m not supposed to die like this, a robot voice in my ear telling me I’m dead. She could feel her breath becoming shallow. She had always heard that suffocating is a painful process, but she had somehow found a way to embrace it. She calmed her breathing and tried to relax as she closed her eyes for the final time.
